source.section: PA-40 lines 1a to 12 (form pages 1-2); PDF page 1 and form line 12 rate 3.07 percent; PDF page 9 no standard deduction or exemptions; PDF page 20 Lines 9 and 10; PDF page 21 Lines 11 and 12; PDF page 11 and PDF page 13 Filing Tip 2 (the plan test has no term on the payer); projection pa_employer_plans covers public_pension_other_state as a reading: another state's government pension is exempt; PDF page 14 Line 2

worked: New York State pension at 63: not a named system, so it is the plan test as a reading; assumed retired after meeting the plan's conditions. Federal AGI = NY state government pension person 0 60,000.00 + interest 20,000.00 = 80,000.00. Federal taxable income = 80,000.00 - standard deduction 15,750.00 = 64,250.00 (given, not tested; the federal senior deduction is ignored). Pennsylvania, as the projection works it: start federal AGI 80,000.00; less 60,000.00 NY state government pension person 0 (pa_employer_plans); income after reliefs = 20,000.00. No standard deduction or exemption (PDF page 9), no Line 10 deduction: state taxable income 20,000.00. Tax = 20,000.00 x 0.0307 = 614.00. No credit in the projection; state income tax 614.00. Form: Line 1a/1c 0.00; Line 2 20,000.00; Line 3 0.00; Line 5 0.00; Line 9 20,000.00; Line 10 0.00; Line 11 20,000.00; Line 12 614.00. Schedule SP: Eligibility Income 20,000.00 is over 8,750.00, so no Tax Forgiveness on the form either. If the reading failed the pension would be taxed above contributions: 1,842.00 on 60,000.00 with none recovered.
accepted_approximations: Pennsylvania has no federal starting point: it adds the positive amounts of eight classes (compensation, interest, dividends, business, gains, rents, estates and trusts, gambling). The mapping runs from federal AGI to those classes: start from federal AGI, then take out what the reliefs below exempt. Wages, interest, dividends, gains, business income and rents are taken as federal AGI holds them, in one sum. The differences that remain are listed one by one in the next four entries.

A New York State pension or any other state's government pension is exempted as an eligible employer-sponsored plan. This is a reading: 'Pennsylvania does not impose income tax on payments you receive that are commonly recognized retirement benefits distributed from eligible employer-sponsored retirement plans' (PDF page 11), and the plan test has no term on the payer, but no sentence names another state's pension. If such a plan were not eligible, it would be taxed above the employee's contributions.
